column4: Registered reports could be highlighted, as well as academic incentives and their relationship to the replication crisis, P-Hacking, and HARKing (all three of which are highlighted). I think special attention could also be paid to animal studies (their issues with replicability, standardization (and whether it's a good thing, see work by Bernhard Voelkl), and generalizability).
column5: P-hacking and HARKing are highlighted, but I think one serious QRP not discussed enough is outlier removal. People often justify p-hacking via removing data by saying the removed data are outliers based on Tukey's Fences, Grubb's, or other tests that are almost always misused with the purpose of p-hacking. In fact, if you go to the reference for Tukey's Fences (Tukey 1976), he DOES NOT SAY that it can be used for data REMOVAL, only flagging data to examine for technical problems in measurements. The widespread use of outlier DETECTION methods for data REMOVAL based purely on statistics without assessing technical problems with data collection is a massive source of false positives. It's very easy to write simulations (I can share code for this if you like) showing that outlier removal leads to higher false positive rates, particularly with the sample sizes typically used in neuroscience studies. This would be a good pedagogical tool. Zooming out, I believe academic incentives to be tremendously detrimental to the trustworthiness of the literature, with registered reports being the simplest and most effective fix *in our current incentive structure*. I believe these issues are just as if not more serious than all of the philosophical issues Konrad raises in his brilliant work on the massive confounding of unmeasured variables in neuroscience studies and misleading causal language.

column5:
Potentially adding a checklist for general areas to assist in the reproduction or clarify data collection methods, materials used, or the methods used for statistical analysis. For example, for items/ materials used, can have general sections to check off such as “technology” “medical equipment” “household items” “power tools” etc and an optional fill-in box with items used (I feel it’s at the author(s) discretion to include or not include materials in fill-in box, but not necessary - the information is readily available, just need to read the paper to find it! The checklist serves as a very quick overview of necessary details that may not be included in the abstract. Also helps address availability of free access to published works if abstract is missing information.)
Also would be helpful to know the author(s) experience in the field and as it relates to the study. 10 years of experience with 2 weeks of experience working with a specific type of equipment or technology, compared to someone with 10 years experience working with the same equipment but 2 weeks in the related position/ role/ industry is important information. Either is fine, but knowing that objective background as it relates to the author(s) can assist in the replication and greater understanding of the study and its entire process.

column4:
- Excessive pressure to publish frequently and in "high impact" journals
- Poor alignment of incentives that rely on "productivity" metrics for career advancement
- Preregistration should be more prevalent, even for preclinical research
- Sources of spurious correlation are not widely recognized, such as conditioning variable selection on a collider relationship
- Incorrectly controlling nontreatment variables by default (e.g., by stratification) without assessing permissive/instructive roles in the causal diagram
- Recognizing and interpreting datasets that exhibit "Simpson's paradox" relationships
- Contrary to common methodologies, "necessary and sufficient" interventions are neither necessary nor sufficient for causal inference in complex biological systems
column5: When people are forced to publish frequently, including and especially as trainees, then it should be no surprise that they do not have the knowledge, experience, or simply the time to harden their scientific interpretations against the myriad hidden or counterintuitive obstacles that experimental data puts in the way of reliable scientific inference. Additionally, replication is severely harmed—no matter how detailed the descriptions of methods and protocols—by the ever-increasing complexity of modern biological methodologies and the consequent reliance on widely shared tools that are understood by few. To summarize: We need to democratize science by simultaneously broadening participation and establishing robust guardrails. To do this, we should discard bullshit productivity metrics, dismantle the traditional for-profit publishers, establish new forms of publication and research dissemination, find ways to assign credit for broad ranges of scientific contributions, switch from pre- to post-publication review automated by recommender systems, and integrate statistical and causal rigor into experimental design, analysis, and modeling from the beginning to avoid the "garden of forking paths" that sets the stage for many of the aforementioned pitfalls and obstacles presented by data. To the latter point, a stronger emphasis on theory—deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning about systems of causes and mechanisms—would serve to provide critical balance against the inherent harms of the excessive reliance on data that pervades modern science.

column5: This definitely seems like a worthwhile effort but I think it i important to distinguish between issues that arise from lack of knowledge and issues that arise from funding realities. For example, one of the options listed is "Planning experiments with reproducibility in mind. (e.g. availability of equipment)". Experimental data will be easier to replicate if the same model of equipment is used in the replication effort as was used in the original experiment. Unfortunately, I know some researchers who can't afford modern equipment and rely on equipment that has been out of production for decades. As a result, the chances that another researcher attempting to reproduce those results would be able to obtain the same model are slim. I'm sure that the original experimenter would love to be working with modern standardized equipment, but that is just no consistent with funding realities. A similar reality exists in regards to sample sizes, which is another option listed. I'm confident most researchers would prefer utilize larger and more comprehensive samples, but just cannot afford to do so.

The incentives. I think that it is important to make people realized that the incentives of academia are not well aligned with rigor in science and that being rigorous requires courage because it is not sufficiently rewarded. In this topic, there should be something on how to sell the fact that someone is a rigor champion (in paper, in grant proposals, etc.)

The law of small numbers/generalization of the results. Many people believe that if they get a significant with N=10, they would also get it with a bigger sample because their significant effect size is so big but they don't realize that their effect size is largely overestimated and that with such sample size, they could only detect large effect size.

Focus on hypothesis testing (Bayesian or frequentist) and not on effect size estimation. In the area of big data, it is easy to get a signficant effect. the question is whether this effect is meaningful. Not every paper needs to deliver a p-value or a Bayesian factor. Some might simply produce an effect size and its related confidence interval.

column4: A factor hugely influencing scientific rigour comes about by the incentives we have in academia - the need to publish a lot in prestigious journals is detrimental to scientific rigour. Moreover, working patterns/organization of scientific work hampers scientific progress - in the 21st century, we need truly collaborative working structures (in large scale) to tackle current science problems. The individual researcher who works on their own problem in isolation, with no other real stakeholders investing a meaningful part of their time and resources in the project, is inefficient, and often detrimental to the researcher's well-being. So to sum up, we need different incentives and different working structures in academia to meet the needs for scientific rigour effectively.
